description: Vocal and physical choices for Hanako, Reiko and Etsuko that age them across two decades.
content_html:
The Challenge of Playing Time

A performer playing Hanako in The Great Wave faces one of the most demanding tasks in any of the nine set plays: she must show a journey from a defiant 17-year-old arguing on a storm-swept beach in 1979 to a woman in her late thirties who has survived captivity, forced re-education, and the slow erosion of her original self. She does this without the aid of sophisticated prosthetics or years of naturalistic preparation — she does it through the precision of vocal and physical choices, scene by scene, across the play’s 24-year arc.

This is not simply about playing “older.” Playing older is a surface effect (slowed movement, deeper voice). What the play requires is something more specific: tracking how Hanako’s relationship to proxemics, to space, to silence, changes as she learns to survive inside a system designed to contain her. The body that moves freely and claims space on the beach is not the same body ten years into captivity. The difference is not just age — it is accommodation.

Key Fact

Playing Hanako across time requires a performer to track three layers simultaneously: age (physical changes in posture, pace, breath); accommodation (how the body learns to move within a system of surveillance); and internal resistance (the private moments where the self underneath the performance emerges). All three must be visible at different moments of the play.

Hanako: Physical Containment and Release

In the beach scene — Hanako’s first appearance and her last moment of freedom — a performer can play her in full ownership of her body: wide stance, blocking that cuts across the stage diagonally, gestures that reach outward. The argument with Reiko in the storm can use full vocal range — high pitch on challenge, fast pace as the argument escalates, volume that competes with the implied sound of the wind. This is a young woman who has not yet learned that her body can be owned by someone else.

The contrast in the first captivity scenes should be stark. Now, the performer might begin reducing the size of every gesture: arms held closer to the body, movements that do not claim more space than strictly necessary, eye-contact that is carefully managed — not downcast (that would signal defeat too early) but controlled, the eye-contact of someone learning when it is safe to look and when it is not. The voice becomes more contained: lower register, measured pace, pauses that are not emotional hesitation but strategic hesitation — calculating what to say rather than feeling unable to say it.

The “release moments” — private scenes where Hanako is not under official observation — give the performer the opportunity to show what is still alive underneath the accommodation. A sudden small physical release (letting the hands open, a brief change in spine alignment) can communicate volumes. These moments should be very short — the accommodation has become second nature, the release is a flash — and they function as a kind of dramatic punctuation, reminding the audience that Hanako is not the role the state has written for her.

The interrogation scenes are some of the play’s most demanding. Hanako is being asked to confirm or deny an identity — to accept a new name, a new history. A performer who plays these scenes by trying to “look scared” misses the point entirely. The more interesting and more truthful choice is stillness: absolute stillness, placed centre stage under a harsh overhead light, with the minimum of facial expression. This choice tells the audience that Hanako is conserving herself — spending as little energy as possible, giving as little as possible, preserving something inside that the system cannot reach.

Vocally, the same principle applies. A flat, even delivery in the interrogation scenes — not dead, but carefully neutral — communicates the same conservation of self. The voice is not the character’s private voice; it is the voice produced for the officials. The distinction between this voice and the rare private voice (warmer, perhaps slightly faster) is something the audience begins to read as the play goes on, so that a shift in vocal register becomes a signal of private self re-emerging.

Reiko: Grief That Does Not Resolve

The performer playing Reiko faces a different temporal challenge: not the gradual accommodation of captivity but the gradual hardening of unresolved grief into something that looks like certainty. Reiko spends the play refusing to accept that Hanako is dead. In the early scenes this refusal is raw — it can be played with a vocal tension that sits high in the chest, a physical restlessness, hands that cannot settle. In the middle scenes, the grief has been lived with long enough that it has taken on structure — it has become a project, an advocacy position. The proxemic patterns change: Reiko moves toward people, demanding to be taken seriously, whereas early-grief Reiko might move away, closing off.

For a performer, the key is never to play the same version of Reiko twice. Each scene must show the accumulation of years. A simple physical marker — the way she holds herself when addressing officials, a very slight brittleness in the voice that was not there at the beginning — communicates the weight of two decades without requiring the performer to play every moment at full emotional intensity.

Etsuko: Resignation That Is Not Defeat

The mother, Etsuko, ages the most visibly of the three central women across the play’s timeline. But the danger in playing her is to reduce her ageing to physical signifiers only (slower movement, quieter voice) without tracking her interior journey. Etsuko’s trajectory is from active maternal grief to something that examiners often describe as “resignation” — but a performer who plays resignation as a collapse misses the point. Etsuko’s silence in the later scenes is not weakness; it is the outcome of having waited so long that the waiting has become her identity. A performer might express this through very deliberate, economical physicality — each movement purposeful, nothing wasted — and a vocal quality that is low and steady, suggesting not defeat but endurance.

Key Fact

All three central performers must show change over time: this is the play’s deepest requirement. Not a single fixed characterisation but a performance in which the audience can feel the weight of 24 years accumulating in the body and voice. Examiners reward answers that track specific changes — not just “she becomes sadder” but “in the early scenes her voice is in the upper register with rapid pace; by the final act the pace is slower and the pitch lower, suggesting the energy of grief has become the quiet weight of endurance.”

A very common performance-interpretation error is to reduce Hanako’s 24-year journey to a single emotional note: sadness, or alternatively resilience. Both are too simple. Hanako’s journey includes defiance, survival, accommodation, moments of real connection (with Jung Sun), moments of private resistance, and eventually the confirmation that her family has known she was alive — a discovery that is not straightforwardly joyful. A performer who has made a specific, evolving set of physical and vocal choices throughout the play will be able to land that final complexity in a way that a performer playing a single emotion cannot. “I would play her as sad” scores at Developing. “In the teaching scenes I would allow a small warmth to enter the voice when addressing Jung Sun — a slightly raised pitch, a fractionally faster pace — as the only moment where the accommodation shows a crack in its surface” scores at Mastering.
exam_tip_html: For “How would you (as a performer) interpret” questions (8 marks), the most penalised error is describing an emotional state without translating it into specific vocal and physical choices. “I would play Hanako as frightened” earns almost nothing. You must specify: the vocal element (pitch — low to signal suppression; pace — measured to signal strategic control; volume — quiet but not shaky) AND the physical element (stillness, proxemics, gesture size, posture alignment) AND the named moment (in the first interrogation; in the beach scene; in the teaching scene with Jung Sun). Every 8-mark answer needs at least one named vocal choice, one named physical choice, and one named moment. For 20-mark extended staging responses, track how the performer’s choices change across the play’s timeline — examiners value answers that show awareness of how a performance must evolve, not just describe a single moment.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Playing Hanako requires tracking three layers across 24 years: ageing (posture, pace, breath), accommodation (learning to contain the body within a system of surveillance), and internal resistance (the release moments that show the self underneath). Each layer needs specific, changing physical and vocal choices scene by scene.
  • Stillness and vocal neutrality in the interrogation scenes communicate Hanako’s strategy of self-preservation — not defeat. The contrast between her contained official voice and her warmer private voice becomes a signal the audience learns to read over the course of the play.
  • Reiko and Etsuko must also show change over time: Reiko’s grief hardening into advocacy and Etsuko’s grief becoming the endurance of long waiting. Neither character can be played as a single fixed emotion — the accumulation of years must be legible in the body and voice.

practice_questions.text: Name one vocal skill a performer might use to show that Hanako is deliberately suppressing her emotions in the interrogation scenes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any appropriate specific vocal skill: e.g. flat/even tone; measured pace; low pitch; controlled volume; strategic pausing.

practice_questions.text: What is stillness as a performance choice, and when might it be particularly effective in The Great Wave?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining stillness as a deliberate choice to remain physically motionless at a significant moment; 1 mark for explaining when it would be effective — e.g. in the interrogation scenes, where Hanako’s absolute stillness communicates self-preservation and controlled concealment of her true feelings.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a performer might use vocal and physical choices to show the difference between Hanako on the beach in 1979 and Hanako in the North Korean compound a decade later.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: specific vocal choice for the beach scene (high pitch, fast pace, full volume on the argument with Reiko; 1); specific physical choice for the beach scene (wide stance, outward gestures, blocking that cuts across the stage; 1); specific contrasting vocal choice for the compound (measured pace, low register, controlled neutrality; 1); specific contrasting physical choice for the compound (contained gestures, arms close to body, movements that do not claim space; 1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Hanako, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to communicate her internal state in the scene when she first confronts her new identity in the North Korean compound. Refer to at least one vocal and one physical choice and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response specifies concrete vocal choices (e.g. flat, even delivery at low volume — not dead but carefully neutral; measured pace with strategic pauses; a slight steadying of breath before each answer) AND specific physical choices (absolute stillness at centre stage; arms at sides, not held defensively; eye contact that is controlled rather than downcast — looking when safe, not when unsafe). The choices are anchored to the named scene (first interrogation) and the effect on the audience is stated: the audience reads Hanako’s stillness and neutrality as a strategy of self-preservation, understanding that she is spending as little of herself as possible. There is awareness of what this choice reveals about character.

Secure: at least one specific vocal and one specific physical choice; named moment; effect on audience present.

Developing: describes how Hanako is feeling (“scared,” “trying to be brave”) without translating feeling into specific vocal or physical choices.

Emerging: says “I would act scared” or similar; no specific choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: Analyse Turnly's intentions in showing the physical and vocal transformation of Hanako across the play's 24-year timeline. What does he want the audience to understand about the effect of captivity on an individual?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: analyses Turnly’s intention to make captivity physically legible — not as melodrama but as a gradual, specific process of accommodation. The response links the performance arc (from the open, claiming physicality of the beach scene to the contained economy of the compound years) to Turnly’s political argument: what the DPRK abductions actually did to real people was not just imprison them but require them to perform a different self so thoroughly that the original self could only appear in private flashes. The analysis shows awareness of the play’s documentary roots and the ethical weight of staging a real person’s experience. Named moments are used (beach scene, first interrogation, teaching scenes, closing scenes).

Secure: identifies the transformation and links it to Turnly’s themes of identity erasure; generally accurate; at least one named moment.

Developing: describes the changes in Hanako without analysing what Turnly intends the audience to understand; effect is implied.

Emerging: retells plot events without analysis of playwright’s intention.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Great Wave. Discuss how you would work with the performers playing Hanako, Reiko and Etsuko to show the passage of twenty-four years in their vocal and physical choices. Refer to specific performance choices for each character and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a specific, differentiated performance brief for all three characters. Hanako: tracks accommodation and private resistance through changing proxemics, gesture size, vocal register, and the contrast between official and private voices across named scenes. Reiko: tracks grief hardening into advocacy — early scenes with high vocal tension and physical restlessness; later scenes with a brittle steadiness and forward-moving proxemics; vocal change from raw grief to controlled insistence. Etsuko: tracks the endurance of waiting — economical physicality, each movement deliberate; low, steady vocal quality that is endurance not defeat; subtle make-up and physical marks of ageing supporting but not replacing the performer’s choices. All choices are specific, named to moments, and linked to audience effect. The response shows directorial intention: these three transformations are the play’s argument about what state violence costs individual human lives.

Secure: at least two characters addressed with specific choices; generally concrete; effect on audience present.

Developing: general suggestions (“she gets older and sadder”) without specific vocal and physical choices; one or two characters addressed.

Emerging: describes what the characters go through rather than how a performer would communicate it; no specific choices.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the key performance challenge in playing Hanako across The Great Wave's 24-year timeline?
options: Memorising a very long role with many costume changes
Tracking specific vocal and physical changes that show ageing, accommodation and internal resistance
Playing a range of emotions including sadness, anger and joy
Maintaining an authentic Japanese accent throughout the play

knowledge_checks.q: What does a performer communicate through stillness in the interrogation scenes of The Great Wave?
options: That Hanako has accepted her new identity
That Hanako is too frightened to move
That Hanako is conserving herself, spending as little of herself as possible
That Hanako is preparing to escape

knowledge_checks.q: A performer playing Hanako on the beach in 1979 might use a wide stance and outward gestures; a decade later in the compound she might use _____ to show how her body has learned to live within a system of surveillance.
Reiko's grief across the play should harden from raw emotion into something that resembles a fixed _____, showing the decades of advocacy and refusal to accept Hanako is dead.
Match each character to the core performance challenge across the play's timeline:
right: Tracking accommodation and private resistance through contained physicality and vocal neutrality
Showing grief hardening into advocacy over two decades
Communicating the endurance of long waiting through economical, purposeful physicality

flashcard_questions.q: What three layers must a performer track when playing Hanako across twenty-four years?
flashcard_questions.a: Ageing, accommodation, and moments of internal resistance.

flashcard_questions.q: What physical choices might show Hanako on the beach at 17?
flashcard_questions.a: Wide stance, outward gestures, blocking that cuts across the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What physical choices might show Hanako a decade into captivity?
flashcard_questions.a: Contained stillness, arms close to body, movements that claim minimal space.

flashcard_questions.q: What is stillness as a performance choice?
flashcard_questions.a: Deliberate physical motionlessness at a significant moment, creating tension or communicating inner state.

flashcard_questions.q: What vocal quality communicates Hanako's strategic self-preservation in interrogation scenes?
flashcard_questions.a: Flat, even tone at low volume — neutral, not emotional.
The physical and spatial relationship between performers, communicating status or emotion.

flashcard_questions.q: How should Reiko's grief change across the play's timeline?
flashcard_questions.a: From raw vocal tension and physical restlessness to a brittle, forward-moving certainty.

flashcard_questions.q: How should a performer play Etsuko's silence in the later scenes?
flashcard_questions.a: As endurance, not defeat — economical physicality, low steady voice, purpose in every movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What vocal signal could show the teaching scenes are different from the interrogation scenes for Hanako?
flashcard_questions.a: A slight warmth — raised pitch and fractionally faster pace — when addressing Jung Sun.

flashcard_questions.q: What does blocking mean in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The planned pattern of performer movement and positioning on stage, created by the director.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is playing Hanako as simply 'sad' across twenty years a weak performance choice?
flashcard_questions.a: It collapses a complex arc into one note, missing defiance, accommodation, resistance, and connection.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a contained vocal quality in performance?
flashcard_questions.a: Using a narrow range of pitch and volume, suggesting suppression or deliberate concealment of feeling.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical and spatial relationship between two performers on stage, used to communicate status, emotional connection, or threat.
The planned pattern of movement and positioning of performers on stage, created by the director to create meaning and guide the audience's eye.
A vocal quality where the performer uses a narrow range of pitch and volume, suggesting suppression, control or a deliberate concealment of feeling.
A deliberate performance choice to remain physically motionless at a significant moment, using stillness itself to create tension or communicate internal state.
The management of physical space between a performer and other cast members, which changes to show shifts in relationship, power, or emotional state.
The deliberate change in a performer’s posture, gait, gesture range and vocal quality to mark the passage of time or a shift in a character’s psychological state.
